# vgc-usage-stats — Specification

Status: **Draft** (2026-10-06). This document is the source of truth for what the
repo does. The implementation plan is built from this file; change the spec first,
then the code.

## 1. Purpose and consumers

Take Smogon's monthly Pokémon Showdown usage stats for VGC formats and turn them
into a spread-level dataset with derived stats.

This is a standalone public dataset. It is not built around any particular
downstream project; consumers adapt to its published contract.

Consumers:

- **Downstream tools in any language** (TypeScript, Python, etc.), such as set
  reconstruction or damage-calc tooling. They read the committed JSON outputs
  directly, so the output contract is language-neutral JSON with published JSON
  Schemas (§4.6). Derived stats come from a pinned pokemon-showdown commit that
  is recorded in every manifest (§5.2, §7), so a consumer that pins the same
  commit gets identical numbers.
- **Human browsing** on GitHub through `summary.json` and the per-month manifest.

## 2. Source data (Smogon)

Root: `https://www.smogon.com/stats/`. Months are `YYYY-MM/` directories, from
2014-11 to the present. A few directories carry suffixes (`-DLC1`, `-H1`/`-H2`),
and none of them matter for Champions formats. A new month appears around the 1st
of the following month (2026-09 was published 2026-10-01).

content.text:
Entire is set up and working here. Two checkpoints exist already, and both are tied to your first commit and your SPEC-writing session.

**What Entire does.** It records your Claude Code sessions and ties them to git commits. The hooks in `.claude/settings.json` capture every prompt, response, and tool call. When you commit, Entire writes the transcript into hidden git refs under `refs/entire/checkpoints/` and adds an Entire-Session trailer to the commit. Those refs ride along with your normal push, so anyone with the CLI can later ask why a line exists and get the original prompt and reasoning behind it. The local branch named `entire/8bad577-e3b0c4` is a temporary shadow snapshot of work since your last commit. Entire manages it, so leave it alone.

**Does that replace committing docs?** Partly. Entire captures the conversation, not your deliverables. Split your docs by purpose:

- **Commit docs that describe the current contract.** Your SPEC file calls itself the source of truth and is written for downstream consumers. That belongs in git where people browsing GitHub can read it. Checkpoint refs are invisible in the GitHub web UI.
- **Skip docs that are just reasoning history.** Plan-mode output, "here's what Claude considered on Tuesday" notes, and scratch design discussions are already in the transcript. Committing them duplicates what `entire why` and `entire checkpoint explain` already give you.

**One thing to be aware of.** The full transcript gets pushed to origin, and this repo is public. Anyone can fetch `refs/entire/*` and read your sessions, including anything you paste into them. Keep anything private out of sessions in this repo. If you would rather transcripts stay local, Entire has a disable option, but then you lose the why-history on push.

**Getting the most out of it:**

1. Fix the stale hooks first. Status reports they are out of date:
   ```
   entire enable --force
   ```
2. Push so the pending checkpoint syncs. One is waiting on your next `git push origin`.
3. Commit in intent-sized chunks. Each commit links to the session work since the previous commit, so smaller commits make `entire why` answers sharper.
4. Log in once so search and the web view work:
   ```
   entire login
   ```
5. Use these day to day:
   ```
   entire why src/foo.ts:42        # prompt and session behind a line
   entire checkpoint explain <sha> # what a commit's session did
   entire search "spread parsing"  # semantic search across sessions
   entire recap --week             # what got done recently
   ```
6. Tell Claude to use it too. Add a line to a CLAUDE.md in this repo saying to run `entire why` or `entire search` before changing code it does not understand. Entire also exposes `entire agent-help` so agents can read exact flags instead of guessing.
